summary.text: Applying Euler’s transformation twice to suitable formal hypergeometric series and comparing the coefficient of \(X^n\) rewrites the sum as \(\sum_k \binom{3n}{n}q_{n,k}\binom{2n-k}{n}^2\), where \(q_{n,k}=0\) for \(2k>n+1\) and otherwise is an explicit factorial ratio. For every remaining term, Legendre’s formula reduces its \(p\)-adic valuation to a calculation with floors \(\lfloor m/p\rfloor\); the bounds \(2p+1\le 3n\) and \(n<p\) make this valuation at least \(3\), and the ultrametric inequality gives the same bound for the sum.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n \binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}\binom{3n+2k}{n}.
\]
We prove that if \(p\ge 5\) is prime and
\[
\left\lceil\frac{2p+1}{3}\right\rceil\le n\le p-1,
\]
then \(p^3\mid a(n)\).

We first derive a finite hypergeometric transformation for \(a(n)\).

For a rational number \(x\) and a nonnegative integer \(k\), write
\[
(x)_k=x(x+1)\cdots(x+k-1),\qquad (x)_0=1,
\]
for the rising factorial. Introduce the formal hypergeometric power series
\[
F(a,b;c;X)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(a)_k(b)_k}{(c)_k k!}X^k.
\]
Only formal power series are involved, so no convergence issue arises.

We need Euler's transformation in the following form. If \(L\) is a nonnegative integer satisfying
\[
L=a+b-c,
\]
with \(c>0\), then
\[
(1-X)^L F(a,b;c;X)=F(c-a,c-b;c;X). \tag{1}
\]
For completeness, this follows directly from the formal hypergeometric differential equation. If
\[
u_k=\frac{(a)_k(b)_k}{(c)_k k!},
\]
then
\[
(k+1)(k+c)u_{k+1}=(k+a)(k+b)u_k.
\]
Consequently \(y=F(a,b;c;X)\) satisfies
\[
X(1-X)y''+\bigl(c-(a+b+1)X\bigr)y'-ab y=0. \tag{2}
\]
Conversely, since \((k+1)(k+c)\ne0\) for every \(k\ge0\), equation (2) determines each coefficient successively from the constant coefficient. Thus a formal solution of (2) is uniquely determined by its constant term. Substituting
\[
g=(1-X)^L y
\]
into (2), using \(L=a+b-c\), and differentiating by the product rule shows that \(g\) satisfies
\[
X(1-X)g''+\bigl(c-((c-a)+(c-b)+1)X\bigr)g'-(c-a)(c-b)g=0.
\]
Its constant term is 1. The series on the right side of (1) satisfies this same equation and also has constant term 1, proving (1).

Apply (1) first with
\[
A=\frac{3n+1}{2},\qquad B=\frac{3n+2}{2},\qquad C=n+\frac12.
\]
Here
\[
A+B-C=2n+1,
\]
and
\[
C-A=-\frac n2,\qquad C-B=-\frac{n+1}{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
(1-X)^{2n+1}F(A,B;C;X)
 =F\left(-\frac n2,-\frac{n+1}{2};C;X\right). \tag{3}
\]
Apply (1) a second time with \(a=b=n+1\) and \(c=1\). Again \(a+b-c=2n+1\), and hence
\[
(1-X)^{2n+1}F(n+1,n+1;1;X)=F(-n,-n;1;X). \tag{4}
\]
Multiplying (3) by \(F(n+1,n+1;1;X)\), and using (4), gives
\[
F(A,B;C;X)F(-n,-n;1;X)
=
F\left(-\frac n2,-\frac{n+1}{2};C;X\right)
F(n+1,n+1;1;X). \tag{5}
\]

We now extract the coefficient of \(X^n\). Two elementary coefficient evaluations are
\[
[X^j]F(-n,-n;1;X)=\binom nj^2 \qquad (0\le j\le n), \tag{6}
\]
because \((-n)_j=(-1)^j n!/(n-j)!\), and
\[
[X^j]F(n+1,n+1;1;X)=\binom{n+j}{n}^2. \tag{7}
\]
Define
\[
q_{n,k}=[X^k]F\left(-\frac n2,-\frac{n+1}{2};n+\frac12;X\right)
=
\frac{(-n/2)_k (-(n+1)/2)_k}{(n+1/2)_k k!}. \tag{8}
\]
Then (5), (6), and (7) imply
\[
\sum_{k=0}^n
\frac{(A)_k(B)_k}{(C)_k k!}\binom{n}{n-k}^2
=
\sum_{k=0}^n q_{n,k}\binom{2n-k}{n}^2. \tag{9}
\]

We next identify the left side with the desired sum. The duplication identity for rising factorials is
\[
(x)_{2k}=4^k\left(\frac x2\right)_k\left(\frac{x+1}{2}\right)_k. \tag{10}
\]
Using (10), together with ordinary factorial expressions for rising factorials, gives
\[
\binom{3n}{n}\frac{(A)_k(B)_k}{(C)_k k!}
=
\binom{n+k}{k}\binom{3n+2k}{n}. \tag{11}
\]
Indeed,
\[
\frac{(A)_k(B)_k}{(C)_k k!}
=
\frac{(3n+1)_{2k}(n+k)!(2n)!}
{(2n+2k)!\,n!\,k!},
\]
and multiplication by \(\binom{3n}{n}=(3n)!/(n!(2n)!)\) reduces this exactly to the product of binomial coefficients in (11).

Multiplying (9) by \(\binom{3n}{n}\), and using \(\binom n{n-k}=\binom nk\), therefore yields the transformed finite-sum identity
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n T_{n,k}, \tag{12}
\]
where
\[
T_{n,k}=\binom{3n}{n}q_{n,k}\binom{2n-k}{n}^2. \tag{13}
\]
Although the individual \(T_{n,k}\) have been written as rational numbers, their sum is the integer \(a(n)\).

We require a more explicit expression for \(q_{n,k}\). Applying (10) with \(x=-(n+1)\) gives
\[
(-(n+1))_{2k}=4^k\left(-\frac{n+1}{2}\right)_k\left(-\frac n2\right)_k.
\]
Since \(2k\) is even, \((-(n+1))_{2k}\) equals the falling factorial
\[
(n+1)^{\underline{2k}}=(n+1)n\cdots(n+2-2k).
\]
A second use of duplication, now with \(x=2n+1\), gives
\[
\left(n+\frac12\right)_k
=
\frac{(2n+2k)!\,n!}{4^k(2n)!(n+k)!}.
\]
Substitution in (8) therefore gives
\[
q_{n,k}=
\frac{(n+1)^{\underline{2k}}(n+k)!(2n)!}
{(2n+2k)!\,n!\,k!}. \tag{14}
\]
In particular,
\[
q_{n,k}=0\quad\text{if }2k>n+1. \tag{15}
\]
If \(2k\le n+1\), then
\[
(n+1)^{\underline{2k}}=\frac{(n+1)!}{(n+1-2k)!}.
\]
Substituting this and the factorial formulas for the binomial coefficients into (13) gives
\[
T_{n,k}=
\frac{(3n)!(n+1)!(n+k)!\,((2n-k)!)^2}
{(n!)^4 (n+1-2k)!(2n+2k)!\,k!\,((n-k)!)^2} \tag{16}
\]
whenever \(0\le k\le n\) and \(2k\le n+1\).

We now impose the hypotheses on \(p\) and \(n\). The lower bound on \(n\) is equivalent to
\[
3n\ge 2p+1, \tag{17}
\]
and the upper bound gives
\[
n<p. \tag{18}
\]
Let \(v_p\) denote the usual \(p\)-adic valuation on nonzero rational numbers, normalized by \(v_p(p)=1\). For every nonnegative integer \(m<p^2\), Legendre's formula gives
\[
v_p(m!)=\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^j}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac mp\right\rfloor, \tag{19}
\]
because all terms with \(j\ge2\) vanish.

Fix \(k\) with \(0\le k\le n\) and \(2k\le n+1\), so that (16) applies. Every factorial argument in (16) is less than \(p^2\). To see this, note that \(n<p\), while
\[
2n+2k\le 3n+1

a nd all the other arguments are at most \(3n+1\). Since \(n\le p-1\),
\[
3n+1\le3p-2<p^2
\]
for \(p\ge5\). Thus (19) applies to every factorial in (16).

We record the required integer quotients. From (17) and \(3n<3p\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{3n}{p}\right\rfloor=2. \tag{20}
\]
Moreover, \(2k\le n+1\) implies
\[
2n-k\ge \frac{3n-1}{2}\ge p,
\]
where the final inequality follows from \(3n\ge2p+1\). On the other hand \(2n-k<2p\). Hence
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{2n-k}{p}\right\rfloor=1. \tag{21}
\]
Also, because \(k\le n<p\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor=
\left\lfloor\frac kp\right\rfloor=
\left\lfloor\frac{n-k}{p}\right\rfloor=0. \tag{22}
\]

Put \(t=n+k\). We claim
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{2n+2k}{p}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{n+k}{p}\right\rfloor+1. \tag{23}
\]
If \(t<p\), then \(t\ge n>p/2\), the latter following from (17), so \(p\le2t<2p\). Thus the two sides of (23) are both 1. If \(t\ge p\), then \(t<2p\), while
\[
2t=2n+2k\le3n+1\le3p-2<3p.
\]
Thus \(2p\le2t<3p\), and the two sides of (23) are both 2. This proves the claim.

Finally, since \(n+1-2k\le n+1\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{n+1-2k}{p}\right\rfloor
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{n+1}{p}\right\rfloor. \tag{24}
\]

Apply \(v_p\) to (16), use its additivity on products and quotients, and then use (19). If we abbreviate
\[
\alpha=\left\lfloor\frac{n+1}{p}\right\rfloor,
\qquad
\beta=\left\lfloor\frac{n+k}{p}\right\rfloor,
\qquad
\gamma=\left\lfloor\frac{n+1-2k}{p}\right\rfloor,
\]
then (20)--(23) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(T_{n,k})
&=2+\alpha+\beta+2\cdot1
 -\bigl(4\cdot0+\gamma+(\beta+1)+0+2\cdot0\bigr)\\
&=3+\alpha-\gamma.
\end{aligned}
\]
By (24), \(\gamma\le\alpha\), and hence
\[
v_p(T_{n,k})\ge3. \tag{25}
\]
For the remaining indices, namely those with \(2k>n+1\), equation (15) says \(T_{n,k}=0\). Thus every summand on the right side of (12) is either zero or has rational \(p\)-adic valuation at least 3.

The nonarchimedean inequality
\[
v_p(x+y)\ge\min\{v_p(x),v_p(y)\}
\]
shows, by repeated addition, that the finite sum in (12) is either zero or has \(p\)-adic valuation at least 3. This sum is \(a(n)\), which is an integer (indeed a sum of nonnegative integer products). Therefore
\[
v_p(a(n))\ge3,
\]
and for an integer this is exactly the statement
\[
p^3\mid a(n).
\]
This proves the conjecture for every prime \(p\ge5\) and every \(n\) in the stated interval.
